6.0.s.en: 1. The king recalls the deeds of Mordecai:

6.0.0.en: "1 On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king. 2 And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's chamberlains, the keepers of the door, who sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. 3 And the king said, What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this? Then said the king's servants that ministered unto him, There is nothing done for him." [1-3].

6.0.1.en: What a wonderful timing! While Esther was preparing the banquet, and it was not easy for her to attack Haman, the king's favorite, and while Haman was spending the whole night preparing a huge cross for Mordecai, God was using all the events together to accomplish His plan of salvation in the most wonderful way. What Mordecai and Esther could not do, the Lord Himself did, taking sleep from the king's eyes so that He might urge him to reward Mordecai for his faithfulness in his work and for saving his life.

6.0.2.en: Here it is fitting for us to pause a little and see the prayers of Mordecai answered at the proper time. When I say his prayers, I do not mean merely the outward words from his mouth, but his whole life. For every spiritual work, every act of faithfulness and every sanctification turns our life into prayers accepted before God. What Mordecai did years ago, when he served the king faithfully and saved him from the wicked plot, was a prayer to God Himself, who accepts every spiritual work and every act of faithfulness as the fragrance of sweet incense. By this we understand the saying of the Psalmist: "But I am prayer" (Ps 109:4), realizing that every member of our body, every emotion and every feeling, when sanctified and striving in the Lord, becomes like an active tongue that opens the gates of heaven to bring us into the presence of God. "The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much" (Jas 5:16), because what his tongue utters in petitions comes forth in harmony with what his whole life proclaims, being itself a prayer. On the contrary, the prayer of the wicked is an abomination before the Lord, because he utters one thing while his life utters another, so that it becomes a discord in which the Lord finds no rest.

6.0.3.en: The Lord answered the prayers of Mordecai, which he offered by his practical life as well as by his tongue. While Haman was perfecting his plan to bring Mordecai down to the dust, behold, God "raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD'S" (1 Sam 2:8).

6.0.4.en: Sleep fled from the king's eyes, and when he remembered the deeds of Mordecai and asked about his reward, according to what he had received, it was nothing, and his heart had no rest until he returned love for love. He realized that Mordecai had saved his life, so what reward would be fitting for such a deed? Truly, if this was the feeling of a king known for his cruelty, what is fitting for us to render to God in return for His love, since He saved us from our deadly sins? As St. John Chrysostom says: [If Mordecai, when the king remembered his services, found them profitable to him and was raised by them to such great glory, how much more does it befit us to be thankful to God and to offer Him abundantly all that we have, when we remember His forgiveness of the sins we committed against Him and the goodness He has shown us!].

6.1.0.en: 4 And the king said, Who is in the court? Now Haman was come into the outward court of the king's house, to speak unto the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him. 5 And the king's servants said unto him, Behold, Haman standeth in the court. And the king said, Let him come in. 6 So Haman came in. And the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself? 7 And Haman answered the king, For the man whom the king delighteth to honour, 8 Let the royal apparel be brought which the king useth to wear, and the horse that the king rideth upon, and the crown royal which is set upon his head: 9 And let this apparel and horse be delivered to the hand of one of the king's most noble princes, that they may array the man withal whom the king delighteth to honour, and bring him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaim before him, Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour.

6.2.0.en: Haman came early in the morning, after a night that he perhaps spent entirely with the carpenters building the cross. He wished to meet the king to ask his permission to hang Mordecai, so that he might enjoy inner peace before delighting in Esther's banquet. Instead he found the king himself asking for him in order to consult him, saying to him: "What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?" [6]. In the pride of his heart he thought that there was no man whom the king loved as he did, so he exaggerated the honor greatly, not realizing that "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Prov 16:18), and that "When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom" (Prov 11:2). As the Father Mar Isaac the Syrian says: [Worldly glory is like a rock hidden in the sea; the sailor does not know it until a ship strikes it, its bottom is torn and it fills with water].

6.2.1.en: He exaggerated the honor and asked that the one loved by the king be clothed with the royal robe and ride the king's horse, with a crown set on the horse's head, as was the custom of the Assyrians and the Persians, and that it be proclaimed before him in the square of the city: Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour.

6.2.2.en: Haman carried the spirit of the devil, whom God honored before his fall, so that he was a cherub with the highest of the heavenly orders, and who in pride wanted to seize for himself what belongs to God. In the same way Haman wanted to seize the king's robe, his horse and his honor!

6.3.0.en: 10 Then the king said to Haman, Make haste, and take the apparel and the horse, as thou hast said, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the king's gate: let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken. 11 Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.

6.3.1.en: The words of the king fell on Haman's ears like a thunderbolt when he said to him: "Do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the king's gate: let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken" [10]. If Haman could not bear Mordecai because of his nationality and his belonging to God, here is the king glorifying and honoring him, calling him "the Jew", and perhaps he learned this during his discussion about his reward.

6.3.2.en: How wonderful! Mordecai humbled himself, so the king raised him to surpassing honor, and Haman's heart exalted itself, so he fell beneath his feet. Because of Mordecai's humility he was raised in order to save their lives and to turn the dark day of their destruction into the joyful feast of Purim, whereas Haman, encouraged by his loved ones, became proud, fell and perished with his sons and all his family.

6.3.3.en: What do we see in the glorified Mordecai but the work of the glorified Christ, who raised us with Him to His glory after He humbled Himself for our sake and cried out on the Cross because of us with a bitter cry? Mordecai put on the royal robe, but the Lord Christ gave us Himself that we might put Him on (Gal 3:27) and be hidden in Him. Mordecai rode a royal horse, but the Lord Christ granted us His divine grace to carry us from glory to glory and bring us to the bosom of His Father. Mordecai received the king's crown, but the Lord Christ granted us in Him the partaking of the divine nature and made us heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ (Rom 8:17); in Him we became the object of the Father's pleasure, and it was proclaimed before us: [Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour].

6.3.4.en: As much as Mordecai was glorified, Haman fell before him until he was under his feet. As the Father Aphrahat says: [Mordecai trod on the neck of Haman his persecutor, and Jesus trampled on His enemies with His feet].

6.4.0.en: 12 And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered. 13 And Haman told Zeresh his wife and all his friends every thing that had befallen him. Then said his wise men and Zeresh his wife unto him, If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him. 14 And while they were yet talking with him, came the king's chamberlains, and hasted to bring Haman unto the banquet that Esther had prepared.

6.4.1.en: "And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered" [12].

6.4.2.en: When Mordecai was honored in the square of the city and received a glory that no one had expected, he returned to the king's house with head held high, but Haman, to whom all used to bow, was ashamed and returned to his house mourning and with his head covered. For a man, covering the head was a sign of intense grief and shame. When David fled from before his son Absalom, "he went up... weeping as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot: and all the people that was with him covered every man his head" (2 Sam 15:30). And when the nobles of Judah were put to shame because of the severe drought and their return from the pits with empty vessels, they covered their heads (Jer 14:3).

6.4.3.en: At any rate, Mordecai returned to the king's house as though it were his own house, since the king had declared him to be beloved to him, and Haman returned to his house full of disgrace and shame. It is as though Mordecai points to the soul glorified in the Lord, victorious by the Holy Spirit, which departs to heaven, "the king's house", as though it were its own house and special dwelling place, whereas the wicked soul that falls like Haman does not return to the life of Paradise but hastens to its own house, that is, to the "ego", and lives shut up in itself, full of grief and shame. It lives with a covering on its head, placing a veil over its mind so that it does not go forth to see the divine things, to behold the heavens and to swim in the eternal realities.

6.5.0.en: Haman returned to his house to meet with Zeresh his wife and his wise men (the sorcerers), who announced his fall to him and thereby crushed his soul even more, for they said to him: "If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him..." [13]. Perhaps they prophesied to him what would come upon him, or perhaps they realized that what they had been dreaming of all night had been turned upside down, and that this could not be mere chance but was accomplished by a mighty hidden hand. Here they felt that what had happened that day was only the beginning of Haman's collapse and of a fall that would continue to the end, so they could not offer him a word of encouragement or hope.

6.6.0.en: It seems that these words crushed him so that he became slow to go to Esther's banquet, for it is said: "And while they were yet talking with him, came the king's chamberlains, and hasted to bring Haman unto the banquet that Esther had prepared" [14].

6.6.1.en: Haman went out to the banquet in a spirit different from the one in which he had received the invitation the day before, for he became like a sheep led to the slaughter. Truly, [it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God] (Heb 10:31), and as the Psalmist says: "The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: in the net which they hid is their own foot taken. The LORD is known by the judgment which he executeth: the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands" (Ps 9:15-16).

7.0.0.en: "So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen." [1].

7.0.1.en: What is this banquet that Esther prepared, at which the king and Haman were to drink, but the banquet of the Cross, which the Church offers to the King, that is, to God, who is pleased with the sacrifice of the Savior and smells it as a sweet savor? Therefore the priest prays: "He who offered Himself as an acceptable sacrifice on the Cross for the salvation of our race, and His good Father smelled it in the evening on Golgotha."

7.0.2.en: If the King drank with joy at the banquet of the Cross and smelled the fragrance of the love of His beloved Son, Haman drank at the same banquet the cup of God's wrath upon him and upon his wicked works. The banquet that gladdened the heart of God with His Church crushed the devil, exposed his deceptions and removed his authority.

7.1.0.en: 2 And the king said again unto Esther on the second day at the banquet of wine, What is thy petition, queen Esther? and it shall be granted thee: and what is thy request? and it shall be performed, even to the half of the kingdom. 3 Then Esther the queen answered and said, If I have found favour in thy sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request: 4 For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage.

7.1.1.en: When the king entered the banquet and drank out of Esther's love for him, he said to her: "What is thy petition, queen Esther? and it shall be granted thee: and what is thy request? and it shall be performed, even to the half of the kingdom" [2]. He calls her by her name and asks her to request even up to half of his kingdom, since he regarded her as his own, his partner in his glory. At the same time he calls her "the queen" to remind her of her royal position, so that she has the right to ask with boldness and confidence, and so to win the king's heart and his glory as well.

7.1.2.en: These are the feelings and words of God to every soul. He calls it by its name as His own special bride, and calls it queen so that it may come to the throne of His grace with confidence (Heb 4:16), and He asks it to gladden His heart by asking Him to take even up to half of His kingdom. Therefore the Lord urges His disciples: "Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full" (Jn 16:24).

7.1.3.en: God longs for every soul to ask Him so that it may receive, for He desires to give it even Himself and to make it an heir enjoying the partaking of His glories. In the face of this surpassing divine love, what does the Church ask, or the human soul as a member of the Church? Like Esther, it asks for neither money nor honor nor any earthly blessing, but it asks for the salvation of its own soul and the salvation of its brethren, for she said: "If I have found favour in thy sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request: for we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage" [3-5].

7.1.4.en: What does Esther ask, when her life and the life of her people were exposed to destruction, slaughter and extermination?!

7.1.5.en: Here Esther stands out as a true mother who embraces all her brethren with love, working and asking for the salvation of all. She did not stand passive before her brethren, but humbled herself, prayed and struggled to the end for their salvation. For the life of faith leads a person out of the ego to live with an open mouth and a heart enlarged for all (2 Cor 6:11). This is what the Apostle declared when he said: "O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged... Now for a recompense in the same, (I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged" (2 Cor 6:11, 13). In the same spirit St. John Chrysostom says: [Nothing makes a person so like Christ as his care for his neighbor], [I cannot believe that a person who does not work for the salvation of his brother is saved], [Nothing is so worthless as a Christian who does not care for the salvation of others... Everyone can help his brother, even if only with good will, if it is not within his power to do anything... If you say that you are a Christian and cannot do anything for others, there is a contradiction in what you say, as if one were to say that the sun cannot give light].

7.2.0.en: 5 Then the king Ahasuerus answered and said unto Esther the queen, Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so? 6 And Esther said, The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman. Then Haman was afraid before the king and the queen.

7.3.0.en: When the king asked about the enemy who had sold Esther and her people to destruction, slaughter and extermination, she said: "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman. Then Haman was afraid before the king and the queen" [6].

7.3.1.en: If the first work of the banquet of the Cross is the salvation of Esther (the Church) and her people, this will be accomplished only through the exposure of wicked Haman and his loss of all authority, so that he stands terrified before God and the holy Church. As St. Paul says: "Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (that is, in the Cross) (Col 2:15). St. John Chrysostom speaks about the Cross, saying: [By it the demons are no longer terrifying but worthless and despised. By it death is no longer death but sleep, for the one who fights us has been cast under our feet].

7.4.s.en: 4. The humiliation of Haman before Esther:

7.4.0.en: 7 And the king arising from the banquet of wine in his wrath went into the palace garden: and Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen; for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king. 8 Then the king returned out of the palace garden into the place of the banquet of wine; and Haman was fallen upon the bed whereon Esther was. Then said the king, Will he force the queen also before me in the house? As the word went out of king's mouth, they covered Haman's face.

7.5.0.en: If the Cross exposed Satan, broke his power and destroyed the death that he brought upon man, so that he was cast down under the feet of the Savior, then he has entered into humiliation before the human being who reigns without him. This meaning was revealed in the fall of Haman at the feet of Esther, who was sitting on the bed, according to the custom of the East in ancient times at banquets... And since the king had gone out into the palace garden, perhaps to think what to do, he returned and found Haman thus in humiliation, entreating while fallen upon the bed, and said: "Will he force the queen also before me in the house?!" [8]. He did not suspect anything, for he knew the bitterness of Haman's soul at that moment, but these words of his came to express his inward fury... They were a sign to those standing by of the king's wrath and put an end to Haman's life.

7.5.1.en: What the king said: "Will he force the queen also before me in the house?!" declares God's view of the true Haman, that is, the devil, who enters the heart of the believer to seize the soul from the hand and bosom of God, as though he were Haman who wished to draw Esther away from the king's bosom and violate her! God is a jealous God; He cannot bear that the enemy should enter His house and snatch His bride from between His hands!

7.6.0.en: 9 And Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon. 10 So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified.

7.6.1.en: When he declared his anger against Haman, "they covered Haman's face. And Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon" [8-10].

7.6.2.en: Thus Haman was justly hanged on the very gallows that he had prepared unjustly for Mordecai, as it is said: "The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead" (Prov 11:8), "The wicked shall be a ransom for the righteous, and the transgressor for the upright" (Prov 21:18), "The wicked is snared in the work of his own hands... in the net which they hid is their own foot taken" (Ps 9:16, 15). "As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head" (Obad 15), "With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again" (Mt 7:2).

7.6.3.en: Satan rejoiced over the Cross and stirred up his helpers to accomplish it, and did not realize that what he was doing would return upon him. As St. Jerome says: [On the Cross Satan and all his host were put to shame; Christ was certainly crucified in the body, and behold, He crucifies the demons on the Cross].
